how-much-to-charge-for-forestry-mulching.text:
← Forestry Mulching Bid Calculator

How much should you charge for forestry mulching?

The honest answer is that price per acre is not a rate, it is a quotient, and the reason is specific rather than philosophical. The machine is paid for by the hour. The acre is what the customer counts. What sits between them is your production rate — acres per machine-hour — and that number is not a property of the lot's size. It is a property of what is standing on it, and across the four densities people actually call about it moves by nine to one. This page prices one real job all the way through, then changes exactly one input to show the problem.

Price your own job →

The job

3 acres of an old pasture growing back in — medium brush, stems 2–4 inches with the odd 6 — on rolling but dry ground. A 75 hp compact track loader with a 6 ft drum mulcher. Operator cost $45/hr burdened, 5 gal/hr of fuel at $3.90, a $1,800 set of teeth lasting 250 hours, a $12/hr service reserve, a $2,400 monthly machine payment, $4,800 a year of insurance, and 70 billable machine hours in an average month. One round trip on the trailer: 2.5 hours and 70 miles at $1.35 a mile. Target margin 35%. Every figure below comes out of the calculator on this site with exactly those inputs.

1. Acres per hour, because it sets everything else

Start at the machine, not the parcel. The rate is swath geometry and nothing more: 

acres/hr = head width (ft) × advance (ft/min) × 60 × cutting share
           ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                        43,560 × passes

A 6 ft head at 42 ft/min while cutting is 15,120 sq ft an hour if you never stopped and the ground were flat. You do stop — repositioning, fuel, walking the boundary, knocking mulch out of the head — so 80% of the hour is cutting; and rolling ground with stumps to steer around slows the advance, here 85% of the quoted speed. One pass. That is 0.236 acres an hour.

Two notes on that number. It is a model, not a measurement: if you have ever timed a finished lot, put your rate in instead and the calculator will tell you what advance speed it implies, which is a better sanity check than any published table. And the “share of the hour cutting” figure is the one people flatter themselves about — it is what separates a clean 5-acre rectangle from a wooded lot cut up by a creek and a driveway.

2. Rate becomes hours, hours become days

3 acres ÷ 0.236 acres/hr = 12.7 machine hours, which at eight machine hours a day is 1.6 days on site. Machine hours is the unit your costs are denominated in. It is also the unit a customer never asks about, which is the whole difficulty.

3. What one machine hour actually costs

Cost of one hour with the drum turning.
LineBasis$ / hr
Operatorburdened$45.00
Fuel5 gal/hr @ $3.90$19.50
Carbide teeth$1,800 set ÷ 250 hr$7.20
Service and repair reservestated$12.00
Payment and insurance($2,400 + $400) ÷ 70 hr$40.00
Total$123.70

The last two lines are the ones a hand-written quote leaves out, and together they are $47.20 of the $123.70 — more than fuel and teeth combined.

Teeth are a consumable, not a repair. A set is consumed over hundreds of hours and the bill arrives months after the jobs that caused it, with no job attached to it, which is exactly why it never makes it into a quote. Clean standing timber is kind to carbide; sand, rock and cutting near grade are not. If you are unsure of the life figure, halve it and look at the price again before you send it.

The payment is a utilisation number wearing a pricing number's clothes. At 70 billable hours a month it is $40.00 an hour — 32.3% of what the machine costs to run. At 160 billable hours the same payment and insurance are $17.50, the hourly cost falls to $101.20, and the same job prices at $2,297.32 instead of $2,737.29. If your per-acre number feels uncompetitive, check that figure before you cut the price: you may be looking at an idle-machine problem rather than a market one.

4. Mobilization is its own line, and that is not a formality

Loading, floating out, unloading, and reversing all of it: 2.5 hours at the operator rate is $112.50, and 70 round-trip miles at $1.35 for truck and trailer is $94.50. $207.00.

That $207.00 is the same $207.00 on a half-acre lot and on a ten-acre one, and this is where a flat per-acre rate does its quietest damage:

LotPrice at 35%$ / acreMobilization share
0.5 acres$721.60$1,443.2029%
3 acres$2,737.29$912.438%
10 acres$8,381.22$838.122%

Same machine, same ground, same margin, and the honest per-acre price runs from $838.12 to $1,443.20 on nothing but lot size. Quote a single number across all three and you have overcharged the ten-acre job you wanted and underbid the half-acre one you now have to drive to. Once mobilization passes about a quarter of the price — which it does at half an acre here — stop quoting that job per acre. A day rate or a stated minimum charge is the honest shape for it.

5. The quote

LineBasisAmount
Machine time12.7 hr @ $123.70$1,572.24
Mobilization2.5 hr + 70 mi$207.00
Total cost$1,779.24
Price at 35% margincost ÷ 0.65$2,737.29

That is $912.43 per acre, with $593.08 per acre as break-even and $958.05 of margin on the job.

Margin is not markup. A 35% margin means price = cost ÷ 0.65. Adding 35% to cost gives cost × 1.35 = $2,401.97, which is a 25.9% margin, not 35%. The gap is $335.32 on this one job, and it repeats on every job you ever quote. This is the most common arithmetic error in trade pricing and it always runs in the same direction.

6. Now change one number

You quote the next lot at the same $1,000 an acre without walking it, because the last one worked out. Same 3 acres, same machine, same costs, same quote — only what is standing on the ground is different:

What is standingAcres / hrMachine hoursYour costBreak-even / acreProfit at $1,000/acre
Light brush, saplings under 2 in0.5065.9$940.71$313.57$2,059.29
Medium brush, 2–4 in0.23612.7$1,779.24$593.08$1,220.76
Heavy brush, 4–8 in0.11226.7$3,508.70$1,169.57-$508.70
Heavy understory, 8–12 in0.05653.4$6,810.40$2,270.13-$3,810.40

$2,059.29 at the top and −$3,810.40 at the bottom: a $5,869.69 spread on one quote. The acreage never moved. What moved is that the same 3 acres is 5.9 machine hours of work in one case and 53.4 in the other — nine times the machine time.

Why it compounds the way it does is worth internalising, because it is two effects, not one:

  • The advance speed falls. Heavier stems mean less forward progress per minute with the drum loaded — here 90 ft/min in saplings down to 30 ft/min in 8–12 inch material, a factor of three.
  • And the pass count rises. Light material falls small enough on the first pass. Heavy material comes down standing on the first pass and the mat then has to be reworked, twice more here, to reach a particle size a customer calls finished. That is another factor of three, multiplying the first.

Three times three is the nine. A customer describing their lot on the phone cannot tell you which of these four rows they are in, and neither “it's a bit brushy” nor a satellite photo will settle it. Walk it.

7. What is not in the per-acre number at all

  • Stumps. Mulching takes standing material down and leaves a mat. It does not remove a stump below grade. If the customer's idea of “cleared” includes grubbing, that is a different machine and a separate line.
  • Stems above what the head is rated for. A 16 inch stem on a head rated to 8 is a felling job before it is a mulching job, and the time to drop it is in no production rate. Price those separately or exclude them in writing — forcing oversized material through the drum is how a day goes to teeth, a belt, or the drum itself.
  • Everything the site says no to. Permits, burn rules, stream and wetland buffers, erosion control, protected species, property lines and buried or overhead utilities. None of it is arithmetic and none of it is in this tool. It is the part of the job that turns a priced quote into a legal one, and it is yours.

What to do with this

  1. Quote the density, not the acreage. Write the stem size and the finish standard into the quote as named terms. A lot that turns out heavier than described is a change order, not a lesson.
  2. Time yourself once. One finished lot with a start and a stop time gives you a production rate worth more than every published per-acre figure put together.
  3. Put the teeth and the payment in the hourly rate before you divide by anything. They are $47.20 of $123.70 here and they are invisible per acre.
  4. Use a minimum charge for anything under about an acre, because the trailer does not care how big the lot is.

Open the calculator →

Worked example, not a rate card. Every figure here comes from the inputs named at the top of this page. Your machine, your ground, your market and your own timings are different, and the point of the calculator is to put your numbers through the same arithmetic rather than to adopt these. The density presets in particular are starting points to overwrite, not survey data.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not forestry, engineering, environmental, legal, tax or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. It does not tell you whether mulching is a permitted or appropriate clearing method on any particular parcel, and it says nothing about permits, burn rules, wetland or stream buffers, erosion control, protected species, or utility and property lines. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, for checking the site yourself, and for meeting every obligation that applies to the work. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

FOR OWNER-OPERATORS BIDDING FORESTRY MULCHING AND LAND CLEARING

Price per acre is the answer, not the question.

The machine is paid for by the hour. What turns that into a per-acre number is your production rate — acres per machine-hour — and that rate is not a property of the lot's size. It is a property of what is standing on it. On the 3-acre example below, one flat $1,000 per acre quote earns $2,059.29 on light brush and loses $3,810.40 in 8–12 inch understory: a $5,869.69 spread on the same quote and the same acreage.

So this works the hours first and reports the per-acre figure last, as the quotient it actually is. Put your own job in. Everything runs in this browser; nothing is uploaded.

How much should you charge for forestry mulching? — the worked example, line by line

Quoting off a flat per-acre number? See this calculator vs. a flat price per acre.

Already run leads and jobs through Aspire? See this calculator vs. Aspire for when each is the right one to reach for.

1. The lot

Density is the input that moves the price most and the one a customer describes loosest. Pick the class that matches what is standing, then correct the speed and pass count below if you know better.

2. The machine and the cut

Advance speed is how fast you move forward while cutting, not how fast the machine travels. Passes is how many times the same ground gets worked before the mat is finished.

3. What an hour of this machine costs

The two lines that go missing from a hand-written quote are the last two: carbide teeth are a consumable, and the payment is owed whether the machine turns or not.

4. Getting there, and what you want to keep

Mobilization is its own line because it does not scale with acreage — the trailer trip is the same length whether the lot is half an acre or five. Margin is taken on the price, not added to cost: 35% is cost / 0.65, not cost × 1.35.

The link carries these figures in the part of the URL after the #, which browsers never send to a server. Send it to a partner, a crew lead, or an estimator and they open this same job, already filled in, and can change any field to test their own numbers.

Your quoted price per acre, on four densities

Same acreage, same machine, same costs, same quote. Only what is standing on the ground changes. This is the table to have open when someone asks what you charge an acre.

Everything else held exactly as entered above.
What is standing Acres / hr Machine hours Your cost Break-even / acre Profit at your quote

Common questions

How much should you charge per acre for forestry mulching?

There is no per-acre number that is right twice, and that is the answer rather than a dodge. The machine is paid for by the hour, so a per-acre price is a quotient: your cost per machine-hour divided by the acres per hour you actually cover on that lot. Cost per hour is reasonably stable for a given machine and operator. Acres per hour is not — it is set by what is standing on the ground, and it varies by more than five to one across the four density classes this calculator carries. Work the hours first and let the per-acre figure fall out of them, which is the order the arithmetic runs in.

Why does the same price per acre lose money on heavy brush?

Because acreage is not what you are being paid to remove. A 6 ft head advancing at 90 ft/min through saplings covers about half an acre an hour on one pass. The same head in 8 to 12 inch understory advances at maybe 30 ft/min and needs three passes to bring the mat down to something a customer calls finished, which is around a twentieth of an acre an hour — nine times the machine time on identical ground. The worked example on this page shows one $1,000 per acre quote on 3 acres earning $2,059.29 on light brush and losing $3,810.40 on the heavy class: a $5,869.69 spread on the same quote and the same acreage.

What production rate should I use — how many acres per hour?

Your own, if you have ever timed a finished lot. The presets here are starting points to argue with, not survey data: real production moves with the carrier's horsepower and hydraulic flow, the head, the species mix, how wet it is and who is in the seat, and it moves by more than the gap between two of these classes. If you know you did three quarters of an acre in four hours, put that rate in and the calculator will tell you the advance speed it implies on your head width, so you can sanity-check it against what the machine feels like. A rate you measured beats a rate anyone published, including this one.

Should mobilization be in the per-acre price?

Not as a per-acre line, because it does not behave like one. Loading, floating out, unloading and doing it again in reverse costs the same whether the lot is half an acre or five, so folding it into a per-acre rate overcharges the big jobs you want and undercharges the small ones you will regret. This calculator keeps it as its own line and tells you what share of the price it is. Once it passes about a quarter of the job, stop quoting that job per acre: a day rate or a stated minimum charge is the honest shape for it.

How much does carbide tooth wear really cost per hour?

Enough to matter, and it is the line most often left out entirely because it arrives as one bill months after the jobs that caused it. Teeth are a consumable, not a repair: divide what a full set costs you by the hours a set lasts and you have a real cost per machine-hour that belongs in every quote. The life figure is the one to be honest about — clean standing timber is kind to carbide and sandy or rocky ground is not, and cutting near grade shortens a set faster than anything else you can do. If you are unsure, halve the life and see what it does to the price before you send it.

Is margin the same as markup?

No, and confusing them is how a job that looked profitable is not. Margin is a share of the price: a 35% margin means price equals cost divided by 0.65. Markup is a share of the cost: adding 35% to cost gives price equals cost times 1.35, which is only a 25.9% margin. On the 3-acre example here that is the difference between quoting $2,737.29 and quoting $2,401.97 — $335.32 left on the table on one job, repeated on every job you ever quote. This calculator takes margin on the price, which is what operators mean when they say it.

What about stumps and stems too big for the head?

They are a different job and they need to leave the per-acre number. Mulching takes standing material down and leaves a mat; it does not remove a stump below grade, and a stem well above what your head is rated for is a felling job before it is a mulching job. The time to drop oversized material is not in any production rate, and forcing it through the drum is how a day goes to teeth, a belt, or worse. Tell the calculator the largest stem on the lot and the rating of your head and it will flag the gap, then price those stems separately or exclude them in writing.

Is any of this uploaded?

No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. Your acreage, your hourly costs, your machine payment, the margin you quote at and the jobs you price are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

Can I send this job to a partner, a crew lead, or an estimator?

Yes — "Copy a link to this job" produces a URL that reopens this page with all twenty-five pricing figures and your deposit, price-hold, and payment terms already entered, so whoever you send it to can change the tooth life, the billable hours a month, or the quoted price per acre to their own numbers and watch the price move. That is more useful than a fixed worksheet, because a second opinion on a bid is a conversation about the inputs. The figures travel in the part of the URL after the #, which browsers never transmit to a server, but they are readable by anyone the link reaches; share it the same way you would share the downloaded worksheet.

vs-a-flat-price-per-acre.html.text:
← Forestry Mulching Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per acre

“$X an acre” is not a price for a mulching job — it is a price for one specific density, quietly applied to every lot that calls in.

What a flat price per acre is

A flat rate per acre is the fastest way to quote forestry mulching or land clearing: multiply the acreage by a number and read off a price. It is the number a landowner holding a competitor's flyer will call and ask you to match, whatever is actually standing on their lot.

The number behind it was set for one density class and then reused for every lot afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the acreage, the mulching head's width, a density class (light brush, medium brush, heavy brush, or heavy timber, or your own timed advance speed and pass count), terrain, machine cost inputs, and mobilization, and it computes hours first, from head width, advance speed, and pass count, then reports the per-acre price last — as the quotient it actually is — for this job, not a generic one.

What a flat price per acre doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/acre on a fence line growing back in and on heavy understory with stems up to 12 inches, even though the second takes more than nine times as many machine-hours per acre to clear. Computes acres per machine-hour from head width, advance speed, and passes for the density actually on the ground, so a denser job costs more per acre than a lighter one.
Has no line for tooth wear, ownership cost per billable hour, or mobilization, regardless of how far the machine has to travel or how many hours a month it actually bills. Prices operator wage, fuel, tooth wear, maintenance, and ownership separately, then adds mobilization as its own line because it does not scale with acreage.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the break-even price per acre and the dollar gap against a flat per-acre rate for each density, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Four lots, the same density-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped defaults (a 6-foot head, 85% terrain factor, 80% cutting efficiency, $45/hr operator, $3.90/gal diesel, a $1,800 tooth set every 250 hours, one mobilization trip, and a 35% target margin) on the same 3-acre lot, quoted at the page's own default flat rate of $1,000 an acre ($3,000 revenue on every row below) and priced at each density class:

DensityMachine hoursThis calculator's break-even costResult at the flat $1,000/acre rate
Light brush, grass and saplings under 2 in5.9$940.71 total, $313.57/acre+$2,059.29 profit, 68.6% margin
Medium brush, stems 2-4 in — the most commonly quoted job12.7$1,779.24 total, $593.08/acre+$1,220.76 profit, 40.7% margin
Heavy brush and small trees, stems 4-8 in26.7$3,508.70 total, $1,169.57/acre−$508.70, a −17.0% margin
Heavy understory, stems 8-12 in53.4$6,810.40 total, $2,270.13/acre−$3,810.40, a −127.0% margin

The $1,000/acre rate is not invented — it is this calculator's own shipped default quote, the number the page shows before you change anything. On its own default density (medium brush) that rate still clears a real margin. Carried onto heavy brush or heavy understory on the same acreage, the identical rate does not know the machine is now running four to nine times slower over the same ground, and it quotes both jobs below their own break-even cost. Run your own lot's density and acreage in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-acre rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is carried from the job it was set on to a denser one without checking, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per acre get a mulching bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is the production rate -- acres cut per machine-hour -- and that rate is set by what is standing on the ground, not by the acreage. Light brush under 2 inches clears roughly nine times faster than heavy understory with stems up to 12 inches on this calculator's own defaults, so the same flat rate that is profitable on a light job can lose money outright on a dense one, and a per-acre number has no way to say which job it is looking at.

What does a flat price per acre usually leave out entirely?

Stem density and size. A quote of dollars per acre treats a fence line growing back in the same as heavy understory with stems up to 12 inches, when the second takes more than nine times as many machine-hours to clear as the first on the same acreage -- production rate, not acreage, is what the machine is actually paid for.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped defaults, a flat $1,000-an-acre quote on a 3-acre lot earns $2,059.29 on light brush -- a 68.6% margin -- but loses $508.70 on heavy brush and $3,810.40 on heavy understory with stems up to 12 inches, a -127.0% margin against a job whose own break-even cost is $2,270.13 an acre.

Is a flat price per acre ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of jobs at nearly the same density, a per-acre rate can land close. The risk is carrying the same rate onto a denser job without re-checking it, because the rate does not know what is standing on the next lot and neither does the estimator until density and stem size are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor, fuel, or equipment rates. It takes the acreage, the mulching head's width, the advance speed and passes for the density you describe, and your own wage, fuel, tooth, maintenance, and ownership costs, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-acre rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Forestry Mulching Bid Calculator to price your own job, read how much should you charge for forestry mulching, or see this calculator vs. Aspire.

No warranty. This free tool is not equipment, safety, legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional, a site visit, or your own insurance and payroll numbers. Verify every figure against your own costs before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number on this page and in the calculator stays on this device; this page names no company, product, or service, so it makes no claim about how anyone else prices a job.

Free and open source. If it wins you a job, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-aspire.html.text:
← Forestry Mulching Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Aspire

Two different shapes: Aspire is an account-based business-management platform for running a land-clearing or landscape company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this forestry mulching job cost, given its acreage, brush density, and machine — before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

Aspire is a cloud business-management platform, founded in 2013 by Kevin Kehoe and Mark Tipton, headquartered in Chesterfield, Missouri. It is built for landscape maintenance and construction contractors, irrigation, snow and ice management, and commercial cleaning companies, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it. It bundles CRM and lead tracking, estimating, scheduling, purchasing, job costing, mobile crew time tracking, invoicing, and accounting and payroll integration into one ongoing subscription account, with a mobile app for crews in the field. Its own plans are tiered by a contractor's annual revenue rather than sold at one flat price, and no dollar figure for any plan is published on its site — pricing is reached by requesting a demo. Aspire's estimating module lets a contractor build a database of production rates and predefined service assemblies, per its own public material, which could in principle be configured for forestry mulching among other services. Aspire's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact tier names or any dollar figure, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category are stated, and no dollar amount for Aspire appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Aspire does, and it needs no setup or configuration for forestry mulching specifically — that math is already built in. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes head width, forward advance speed while cutting, the number of passes needed to finish the mat, a terrain factor, and the share of the hour actually spent cutting, and derives a production rate in acres per machine-hour from them. Cost per machine hour is built from operator time, fuel at load, carbide tooth wear spread over the life of a set, a service reserve, and the machine payment and insurance spread over billable hours a month, with mobilization kept as its own line because a trailer trip does not scale with acreage. It reports machine hours, days on site, total cost, the price at a target margin, price per acre and break-even per acre, price per machine hour and per day, and a side-by-side of the same acreage at four brush density classes against one flat quoted price per acre — plus a printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a land-clearing or landscape company and need leads, estimates, scheduling, purchasing, and invoicing tracked in one system across every crew and every job.Aspire, or a comparable business-management platform — running the whole operation is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this forestry mulching job, given its acreage, brush density, and my machine's specs?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account, and forestry-mulching-specific math already built in.
How much does moving from light brush to heavy timber actually change the price, beyond a flat per-acre bump?This calculator's four brush-density-class side-by-side — production rate moves by roughly nine to one across the range a customer's own description implies.
Is my carbide tooth wear actually budgeted into the price, or is it coming out of margin unnoticed?This calculator's own flag for unbudgeted or optimistic tooth life — a cost most flat per-acre quotes never separate out.
I need my whole crew scheduling, purchasing, and job costing running from one shared account across the season.Aspire — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a forestry mulching bid actually work?This calculator's own worked example, line by line.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Aspire?

They do different jobs, and a land-clearing or landscape company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Aspire, founded in 2013 by Kevin Kehoe and Mark Tipton and headquartered in Chesterfield, Missouri, is a cloud business-management platform built for landscape maintenance and construction contractors, irrigation, snow and ice management, and commercial cleaning companies, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it. It bundles CRM and lead tracking, estimating, scheduling, purchasing, job costing, mobile crew time tracking, invoicing, and accounting and payroll integration into one ongoing subscription account, with plans tiered by a contractor's annual revenue rather than one flat price, and no dollar figure published for any plan -- you request a demo to get a quote. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from head width, forward advance speed, passes needed, terrain factor, and the share of the hour actually spent cutting, it derives a production rate in acres per machine-hour, builds cost per machine hour from operator time, fuel at load, carbide tooth wear, a service reserve, and the machine payment and insurance spread over billable hours, and keeps mobilization as its own line since a trailer trip does not scale with acreage. It reports machine hours, days on site, total cost, the price at a target margin, price per acre and per machine hour, and a side-by-side of the same acreage at four brush density classes against one flat quoted price -- before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A land-clearing or landscape company that already tracks leads, schedules crews, and invoices across a whole season is better served by Aspire or a comparable platform; an operator who wants an instant, private answer to what one forestry mulching job should cost from its acreage, brush density, and machine is in the right place here.

Does Aspire price a forestry mulching job the way this calculator does?

Aspire's own public material describes building a database of production rates and predefined assemblies for common landscape services inside its estimating module, which a contractor can configure for whatever services they sell, forestry mulching included. This calculator is not a configurable estimating module -- it is a single-purpose worksheet built specifically around forestry mulching's own physics: head width, forward advance speed, number of passes to finish the mat, terrain factor, and a separate carbide-tooth-wear line most flat per-acre quotes never budget for at all. A contractor who wants one system holding estimates for every service line they sell, tied to CRM and job costing, is better served by Aspire; an operator who wants a free, instant, already-built forestry mulching production-rate model with no setup is in the right place here.
